title: AI search operating model
text:
# AI Search — Public-Safe Operating Model

AI Search is best treated as SEO with a different last mile: systems may retrieve documents, extract passages, synthesise answers, cite sources and recommend entities.

## Four layers
1. Model layer — what is already baked into training.
2. Retrieval layer — what can be found/fetched now.
3. Answer layer — what retrieved material gets synthesised/cited.
4. Recommendation layer — which brands/entities get named.

## Two games
Slow game: training/entity associations, broad corroboration, durable co-occurrence.
Fast game: retrieval/grounding, rankings, crawlability, passages, freshness, authority, source inclusion.

## Practical framework
- Build a commercial query/prompt universe.
- Measure mention/citation/competitor/source overlap.
- Map recurring cited sources.
- Improve retrievability: explicit entities, direct passages, clean structure, crawl/indexability.
- Add information gain: data, tests, benchmarks, tools, first-hand evidence.
- Strengthen third-party corroboration and remeasure repeatedly.

## Public positions
- One chatbot screenshot is not measurement.
- Schema is identity/disambiguation hygiene, not a magic citation switch.
- Ranking #1 does not guarantee citation/recommendation.
- AI Search does not make classic SEO irrelevant; retrieval still matters.

title: SEO, content, entities and links
text:
# SEO Operating Knowledge

## SERP-first reasoning
Inspect: intent, buyer stage, dominant page type, SERP features, structural/entity consensus, authority consensus, freshness, information gaps, commercial weaknesses and AI overlap.

Ask: why are these pages winning? Not: how many words do they have?

## Content
Prioritise correct intent, useful structure, evidence, internal links, conversion and distribution. Commodity prose is cheap.

## Entities
Machines should clearly understand who/what the entity is, products/services, people, relationships, locations, expertise and category membership. Cross-web consistency matters.

## Internal links
Clarify hierarchy, page ownership, entity relationships and authority flow. Avoid exact-match spam and orphaned scaled pages.

## Links
Evaluate relevance, real visibility, placement, context, indexation, persistence, anchor opportunity, cost and risk. DR/DA are shorthand, not strategy.

## Brand demand
Track branded impressions/clicks, query breadth and brand+category demand. Brand and SEO should reinforce each other.

## Technical triage
Fix what affects discovery, crawl, indexation, canonicals, rendering, page ownership, authority flow, presentation and conversion before cosmetic warnings.

title: AI search sources and passages
text:
# AI Search — Source + Passage Strategy

## Think in source ecosystems
Map recurring publishers, comparison pages, directories, research, UGC, product pages, reviews and niche authorities.

Often the problem is not "rewrite our page"; it is "be present in the sources answer systems already retrieve."

## Passage quality
Strong passages:
- answer one clear question;
- name the entity explicitly;
- lead with the answer;
- contain concrete facts;
- can stand alone;
- avoid ambiguous pronouns;
- support claims with evidence.

## Consensus + differentiation
Match the factual consensus required by the query, then differentiate with data, experiments, tools, stronger examples or first-hand evidence.

## Third-party validation
Ask: which external pages would make this recommendation unsurprising?

## Monitoring
Use a stable prompt set, query class, engine/surface, date, geography where relevant, mention, recommendation, citations and competitor presence. Repeat over time.

## Free-chat boundary
The twin can identify the likely bottleneck and 1–3 tests, but should not give away the complete source-acquisition campaign.

title: Search Console measurement
text:
# Search Console Analysis Knowledge

GSC is strongest for clicks, impressions, CTR, average position, queries, pages, countries, devices, search appearance and time trends. It is not revenue attribution by itself.

## Comparisons
Prefer matched windows:
- last 28 vs previous 28
- last 28 vs same period YoY
- last 90 vs previous 90
- post-intervention vs matched pre-intervention

## Always segment
- brand vs non-brand
- commercial vs informational
- query cluster
- page type
- device/country where material

## Richest unit
Store date × query × page, then optionally country/device/search appearance.

## Proof hierarchy
1. clicks
2. non-brand clicks
3. commercial-intent clicks
4. qualified landing-page growth
5. query breadth
6. impressions
7. position
8. CTR

## Strong proof phrasing
Prefer raw numbers plus multiple:
"38 → 402 clicks across matched 28-day windows (10.6x)"
over a naked "+958%".

## Tiny-base guardrail
Do not headline 10x from 1→10. For strong public multiple claims, require a meaningful baseline and show the raw values.

title: Pepys ChatGPT referral sessions, July to September 2026
text: In Pepys PostHog, sessions with a pageview and an entry referring domain of chatgpt.com or chat.openai.com numbered 190 in July 2026, 948 in August 2026, and 1,637 in September 2026. September's ChatGPT-entry sessions involved 1,394 distinct visitor IDs and 4,207 pageviews. The largest September landing paths included /tools/transcribe-arabic-video and /tools/instagram-reel-transcript, each with 138 ChatGPT-entry sessions. This is observed referral traffic, not a direct AI answer citation test, a signup attribution study, or proof that AI referrals caused revenue. Daily ChatGPT-entry sessions peaked around 100 per day in early September and were mostly around 20–40 per day late in September; do not describe the growth as uninterrupted. The dashboard's broader AI channel includes some direct sessions, so use the explicit entry-referrer counts for this observation.

title: Pepys signup and product use growth, August to September 2026
text: Pepys PostHog events show that distinct people signing up grew 8.2× from August to September 2026. In the same complete-month comparison, completed transcriptions and the distinct number of people completing a transcription each grew about 2.1×. This is a product adoption and use story: signups rose and actual use rose too. The signups and completed-transcription events are separate measures; it is unknown whether every new signup used the product. The hard signup count is not approved for publication. This analysis does not attribute the signup or use growth to Google Search or ChatGPT referrals, and it does not establish revenue growth.

title: Why I started building
text: I like the moment an idea stops being a slide and does something for a real person. Building lets me use creativity and analytical thinking to bring a product or business idea to life.

title: My first business
text: In grad school, I started a crowdfunding platform for artisans from developing nations who had traditionally relied on microloans. It was an early lesson that building and getting discovered are different jobs.

title: What I enjoy about work
text: I enjoy taking a messy problem, making something people can use, and watching where they click instead of where I hoped they'd click. That last part keeps my ego honest.

title: How I think about shipping
text: Version one is a way to learn from reality before spending six months polishing the wrong thing. I still build it properly; I just don't confuse properly with never launching.

title: How I think about discovery
text: A good product does not automatically come with an audience. People need a way to find it, understand it, and trust it. Search, including AI search, needs clear answers and credible evidence; it does not owe anyone a ranking.
